body: SALAH-UD-DIN, J.- Through this single judgment, we intend to decide Criminal Appeal No. 189-M of 2025, titled “Iqbal v. State & others,” along with the connected Criminal Appeal No. 226-M of 2025, titled “Muhammad Khitab & others v. Israr & others.” Both appeals arise out of the same judgment dated 22.07.2025, rendered by the learned Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din Additional Sessions Judge-VI/Judge, M.C.T.C./ I.Z.Q., Swat, in Sessions Case No. 42/7 of 2022, arising out of FIR No. 305, dated 21.03.2022, registered U/Ss 302 and 34, P.P.C., R/W section 19- AA, at Police Station Mingora, District Swat. Upon conclusion of the trial, the learned trial Court convicted and sentenced the appellant, as follows:- “(i) Under Section 302(b) PPC to death, who shall be hanged from his neck until he is dead, confirmed and certified by an authorized medical officer in the presence of Magistrate, further subject to the death penalty is confirmed by the Honorable Peshawar High Court.

(ii). The accused is also sentenced to pay an amount of Rs.500,000/- as compensation to the LRs of deceased as provided under section 544-A CrPC. In case of default, he shall further undergo 6-months simple imprisonment. The amount of compensation shall be recoverable as arears of land revenue.
(iii) Under section 19-AA. the accused Iqbal son of Momin is also hereby convicted and sentenced to fine of Rs. 3000/-, In case of default, he shall undergo one-month simple imprisonment.
24. Benefit under section 382-B Cr.PC extended in favor of the accused/convict.

25. The death reference within the meaning of section 374 of the Criminal Procedure Code be compiled and forwarded immediately to the Hon'ble Peshawar High Court, Mingora Bench Dar-ul-Qazal, Swat for confirmation or otherwise of the death sentence.

26. Case property/pistol/crime weapon stands confiscated to state, while the license issued in the name of accused/convict stands cancelled. A notice to the concerned authority be issued to cancel the arms license, regarding the subject pistol 30 bore, issued in the name of accused Iqbal son of Momin Khan. Rest of the case property be kept intact till the expiration of period of appeal/revision, whereafter, it be disposed of accordingly as per law.”

2. The arguments advanced by the learned counsel for the parties, as well as the learned Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din Additional Advocate General appearing on behalf of the State, were heard in detail, and the requisitioned record was perused with their able assistance.

3. As per the prosecution case, the complainant, Muhammad Khitab, reported the occurrence to the local police at the Emergency Ward of Saidu Sharif Hospital, stating therein that, on the fateful day, his sister, Mst. Bakhti, and minor nephew, Hubaib, after appearing before the Court at Gul Kada, Swat, were proceeding towards their house situated at Sakhakot. When they reached the place of occurrence, i.e., Shahi Road near Sohrab Khan Chowk, and were about to board a rickshaw, the accused, namely, Iqbal (the appellant herein), Israr and Momin Khan (acquitted co-accused), arrived there on a motorcycle. The appellant, Iqbal, took-out a pistol and opened fire upon his sister, Mst. Bakhti, hitting her on the head and causing her a serious injury. The occurrence was allegedly witnessed by the complainant himself and his minor nephew, Hubaib. The motive behind the occurrence was stated to be that Mst. Bakhti had previously contracted marriage with Momin Khan, father of the present appellant. Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din However, owing to strained relations between the spouses and their subsequent separation, she solemnized another marriage with Muhammad Diyar. In this regard, a family suit was pending adjudication before the learned Family Court at Gul Kada, Swat. On the basis of the complainant's report, Murasila (Ex.PW-1/2) was prepared, which subsequently led to the registration of the instant FIR (Ex.PW-5/1) against the appellant and his co-accused at the police station concerned.

4. In criminal jurisprudence, the place of occurrence constitutes a material circumstance, particularly for determining the probability of the prosecution version, the presence and availability of eyewitnesses, and the nature of the locality where the incident allegedly took place. In the instant case, the Murasila and the ensuing FIR disclose that the occurrence took place on Shahi Road, Mingora, near Sohrab Khan Chowk, a busy and densely populated locality surrounded by commercial establishments. As per the prosecution's version, the appellant, accompanied by his co-accused, i.e., his father and brother, reached the place of occurrence on a Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din motorcycle. The appellant allegedly drew a pistol and fired a shot at the head of his stepmother, Mst. Bakhti, who subsequently succumbed to the injury sustained by her. The alleged occurrence, having taken place on a public thoroughfare in Mingora, was apparently capable of being witnessed by persons present in the vicinity, including the complainant and his minor nephew, Hubaib. A perusal of the site plan (Ex.PW- 11/1) reveals that points Nos. 1, 2 and 3 were earmarked for the complainant, Muhammad Khitab, the minor eyewitness, Hubaib, and the deceased, Mst. Bakhti, respectively, whereas points Nos. 4, 5 and 6 denoted the respective positions of the appellant and his two co-accused. The crime scene was further examined by the investigating agency, which secured blood-stained earth and one crime empty of a .30-bore pistol through recovery memo (Ex.PW-10/1). In addition, a motorcycle, allegedly used by the accused party for reaching and leaving the scene of occurrence, was taken into possession vide recovery memo (Ex.PW-10/3). The prosecution also relied upon the recovery of a .30-bore pistol, allegedly used in the commission of the offence, at the instance of the appellant, as documented in recovery memo Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din (Ex.PW-10/2). The aforesaid circumstances constitute part of the prosecution evidence concerning the site of the occurrence, the alleged mode of transportation, and the purported recovery of the weapon of offence. The prosecution has further invoked the previous matrimonial relationship between the deceased and the appellant's father, coupled with the subsequent marriage and pending family litigation, as the motive underlying the crime. Nonetheless, the mere establishment of the place of occurrence or the recovery of incriminating articles does not, by itself, conclusively establish the identity of the assailant or his culpability. The probative value of such evidence must, therefore, be appraised in the light of the ocular account, the chain of circumstances, and the other material brought on record.

5. The complainant, Muhammad Khitab, stepped into the witness-box as PW-3 and, while deposing on oath, substantially reiterated the version set-forth in his initial report, embodied in the Murasila and the subsequent FIR. He attributed a specific and unequivocal role to the appellant, Iqbal, alleging that he had fired a fatal shot at his Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din deceased sister, Mst. Bakhti, thereby causing her death. Despite an extensive cross-examination at the hands of the learned defence counsel, the material particulars of his testimony concerning the presence of the parties at the place of occurrence and the specific role attributed to the appellant remained substantially intact. During cross-examination, the complainant maintained that the appellant and his co-accused, Israr, escaped from the scene on their motorcycle, whereas Momin Khan fled on foot. He further disclosed that, on the day of occurrence, Muhammad Diyar, the second husband of the deceased, was in Saudi Arabia, having been granted exemption from appearance by the Court in a criminal case titled “State v. Muhammad Diyar”. He also admitted that the said criminal case had been instituted at the instance of complainant Momin Khan, who had nominated the present complainant i.e. PW-3, the deceased, Mst. Bakhti, and her second husband, Muhammad Diyar, as accused persons. The prosecution also examined Hubaib, the minor son of the deceased, aged approximately nine years, as PW-4. In his deposition, he stated that, on Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din the day of occurrence, he and his deceased mother had travelled from Sakhakot to the Court at Gul Kada, Swat, where his maternal uncle, the complainant, had already arrived, and all three subsequently met there. His account, however, differed slightly from that of the complainant regarding the presence of the accused at the place of occurrence. According to the minor witness, the appellant, Iqbal, and his brother, Israr, arrived at the spot on a motorcycle, whereas their father, Momin Khan, was already present there. Conversely, the complainant had stated in the Murasila that all three accused had arrived at the place of occurrence on a motorcycle. This inconsistency, relating to the mode of arrival of the accused, must be examined in the light of the entire prosecution evidence. However, such a discrepancy, by itself, cannot be regarded as fatal unless it materially affects the substratum of the prosecution case, particularly when the witness was a child of tender years who had allegedly witnessed the violent death of his mother at the hands of a close relative. Such a lapse of memory on the part of a child of such tender age is quite Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din natural and cannot, by itself, be construed as a material contradiction affecting the credibility of his testimony. During cross-examination, the minor witness categorically denied the suggestion that he had implicated the accused at the instance or under the influence of his maternal uncle, i.e. the complainant, or that he was unaware of the identities of the nominated persons. Rather, he explained that he had seen the appellant, Iqbal, Israr and Momin Khan within the Court premises on the day of occurrence and had become familiar with their identities over the preceding month, as they frequently attended the Court in connection with the pending litigations. He further stated that, after leaving the Court premises, they waited for a considerable period for arrival of Rickshaw. Although the minor witness could not recall the name of the particular chowk, however, he described the locality as being surrounded by shops, a description that finds support from the site plan prepared by the Investigating Officer. He further maintained that, immediately after the occurrence, the appellant, Iqbal, and his brother, Israr, fled from Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din the spot on their motorcycle, whereas Momin Khan made his escape on foot. In this material particular, his deposition remained consistent with the complainant's account, thereby lending assurance to their respective versions regarding the subsequent conduct of the accused. The minor witness also delineated the relative positions of the persons present at the scene, stating that Israr was seated on the motorcycle on the opposite side of the road, the appellant was standing in the immediate vicinity of his deceased mother, and the complainant was positioned to her left. This description assumes relevance in assessing the opportunity available to the witness to observe the occurrence and identify the assailant.

6. It is a settled principle of appreciation of evidence that the testimony of a child witness is to be scrutinized with particular care and caution, having regard to the possibility of tutoring, external influence or an imperfect understanding of the events witnessed. Nevertheless, the rule of prudence does not render the evidence of a child witness inherently unreliable, nor does his tender age Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din constitute, by itself, a lawful ground for discarding his testimony. The decisive consideration remains whether his deposition, upon close scrutiny, inspires confidence and finds assurance from the surrounding circumstances. In the case in hand, the prosecution relies upon the fact that the minor witness identified and named the appellant during his initial interaction with the investigating agency. The evidentiary significance of this circumstance must, however, be assessed in the light of the actual contents and timing of his earliest statement and the other material available on record. Likewise, the possibility of tutoring cannot be excluded or accepted merely on the basis of the relationship between the witnesses; it must be evaluated with reference to the circumstances in which the statement was made, the consistency of the account on material particulars, and the existence or absence of any demonstrated influence. Subject to this assessment, if the minor witness's account withstands scrutiny and remains consistent on the essential features of the occurrence, his testimony may lawfully furnish the basis for a finding of guilt, even in the absence of independent Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din corroboration. In respect of pre-requisites of testimony of a child witness, reference can be made to the judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan rendered in the case of “Raja Khurram Ali Khan & 02 others v/s Tayyaba Bibi & another”, wherein it was held that “the essential conditions for a child, or for any person, to appear and testify as a witness, under Art.3 of the Qanun-e- Shahadat Order, 1984 was that the child or the person must have the capacity and intelligence of understanding the questions put to him, and also be able to rationally respond thereto. Such threshold was referred to as passing the "rationality test", and the practice that had developed with time was for the same to be carried out by the presiding Judge prior to recording the evidence of the child witness. Supreme Court observed that the "rationality test", which was applied by the presiding Judge at the commencement of the examination-in-chief of a child witness, should be made applicable throughout the testimony of the child witness; that if at any stage, the presiding Judge observed any hindrance or reluctance in the narration of events, the evidence Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din should be stopped, and remedial measures should be taken to ease the stress and anxiety the child witness might be under, and if required, the case be adjourned to another date; and, that in case the child witness was still unable to narrate his testimony with ease, then the presiding Judge ought to record his findings on the demeanor of the child witness, conclude his evidence, and relieve him as a witness” [ ]. Likewise, in case titled “Mst. Razia alias JIA v/s State” the august Supreme Court of Pakistan had earlier expounded the aforesaid proposition of law in term that “the testimony of a child witness cannot be discarded merely on account of his tender age, provided that he possesses sufficient intelligence to understand the questions put to him and furnish rational answers” [ ]. In the case of “Muhammad Ilyas v. Kabir Hussain”, it was declared with a high degree of legal conviction that there is no hard and fast rule for determination of competency of a child witness[ ]. As a matter of legal requirement, it is the intelligence of a child witness to testify in the “Raja Khurram Ali Khan & 02 others v/s Tayyaba Bibi & another” reported as PLD 2020 S.C. 146

2. Mst. RAZIA alias JIA v/s State” reported as 2009 SCMR 1428 “Muhammad Ilyas v/s Kabir Hussain reported as 2003 YLR 806. Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din circumstances of a given case and not the factor of his or her age. Zatoon Bibi v. State (1998 P Cr. LJ 1680). Similarly in case titled “Muhammad Jamal and others v. State” (1997 SCMR 1595), the august Supreme Court upheld convictions founded, inter alia, upon credible testimony of child witnesses, which derived assurance from other evidence on record. With regard to the testimony of the minor witness in the instant case, the circumstances on record present an exception to the general rule of cautious scrutiny, as his deposition, despite minor discrepancies, remained consistent on the material particulars of the occurrence. In case titled Maqsood Khan v. State (1982 SCMR 757), the Court recognized that a child of tender years cannot reasonably be expected to observe and retain every minute detail of an occurrence. Consequently, a minor discrepancy concerning a peripheral detail, such as the precise mode of arrival of the accused, does not necessarily impair the credibility of a child witness where his account remains trustworthy on the material particulars of the occurrence. The decisive consideration is whether the discrepancy Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din affects the substratum of the prosecution case or creates a reasonable doubt regarding the identity and role of the accused. Lastly, in Muhammad Yakub v. State, reported as 1969 SCMR 235, the august Supreme Court upheld the conviction and sentence of the principal accused, placing reliance upon the testimony of a child witness. The said precedent lends support to the settled proposition that the testimony of a child witness, if found trustworthy and confidenceinspiring upon careful scrutiny, may constitute a lawful basis for maintaining a conviction. The relevant observation of the august Court is reproduced hereunder:- “Iftikhar also gave evidence about the visits of the appellant to his mother in the absence of his father and also about his visit to their house on the evening before the occurrence and the drinking sessions between his father and the appellant. It is a merit of the prosecution case that Iftikhar is not introduced as an eye-witness of the attack by the appellant which could easily be done. His statement was confined to what he had seen and heard without any false exaggerations. Mst. Tasnim was also supported by the evidence of the neighbours who had come to the spot on hearing the noise. They had seen the deceased in a pool of blood and had heard Mst. Tasnim and Zubeda crying and charging the appellant for the murder of the deceased. The learned counsel for the appellant contended that there was a possibility that Mst. Tasnim named the appellant getting the clue from Mst. Zubeda without having herself seen the assault. This argument is merely conjectural and ignores the statement of the neighbours who stated Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din that they found Mst. Tasnim in the street making an outcry immediately after the occurrence and naming the appellant. There is not a word of suggestion that these witnesses are hostile to the appellant in any manner.”

In view of the principles enunciated in the aforementioned judgments of the superior Courts, the testimony of the minor witness, Hubaib, who was approximately nine years of age at the time of recording his statement, cannot be discarded merely on account of his tender age or minor discrepancies in his deposition. His presence alongside his deceased mother at the time of occurrence and his account of having witnessed her tragic death find support from the material particulars of the prosecution case. Significantly, the witness was familiar with the identities of the nominated accused, particularly the appellant, Iqbal, to whom he attributed the specific role of firing a pistol shot at his mother. His testimony, when examined in its entirety and in conjunction with the surrounding circumstances, inspires confidence regarding his presence at the scene and his identification of the appellant as the sole assailant.

7. Even otherwise, in criminal jurisprudence, the appraisal of ocular evidence necessitates its examination with reference to three Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din distinct stages i.e. (i) the events/circumstances leading to the occurrence; (ii) the occurrence itself; and (iii) the circumstances attending the aftermath of the occurrence. The testimony of a witness is required to be scrutinized in this perspective. Any omission or discrepancy concerning the introductory circumstances, such as the manner in which the accused persons reached the place of occurrence or their presence therein, ordinarily relates to collateral matters and does not, per se, detract from the evidentiary worth of the substantive account. Such inconsequential variations cannot be accorded undue significance so as to discredit the prosecution case. The pivotal consideration, however, is the second stage, which encompasses the actual perpetration of the crime. In this regard, the evidence must withstand close judicial scrutiny, particularly with respect to the identity and number of assailants, the individual role ascribed to each accused, the weapon allegedly employed and the specific overt act attributed to each of them. Any material discrepancy touching upon these essential features of the occurrence may render the ocular account unsafe for reliance. Similarly, discrepancies relating to the post-occurrence Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din circumstances, unless having a direct bearing upon the genesis or manner of commission of the offence, are ordinarily of little consequence. In this view of the matter, discrepancies pertaining to collateral circumstances, whether antecedent or subsequent to the occurrence, cannot be treated at par with contradictions concerning the actual commission of the crime. The determinative test is whether the ocular account, qua the occurrence itself, remains consistent, unimpeachable and confidence-inspiring on material particulars, so as to furnish a safe basis for sustaining conviction. In the case in hand, although certain discrepancies are discernible in the depositions of the complainant and minor prosecution witness Hubaib, however, a closer scrutiny reveals that such variations predominantly pertain to collateral circumstances preceding the occurrence, particularly the manner and sequence of arrival of the complainant-party and the accused-party at the place of occurrence. Similar is the position with regard to certain post-occurrence circumstances. These discrepancies, having no material bearing upon the actual commission of the offence, do not furnish any valid ground to discard or discredit the otherwise natural and confidence- Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din inspiring testimony of the child witness. Her presence alongside her deceased mother at the relevant time and place was quite natural and consistent with the attending circumstances. Therefore, such peripheral variations cannot be permitted to detract from the evidentiary worth of his account regarding the actual occurrence i.e. the gruesome murder of his deceased mother, which he had witnessed with his own eyes.

8. During the course of arguments, learned counsel for the appellant placed considerable reliance upon the alleged inconsistencies in the depositions of the prosecution witnesses concerning their appearance before the Court in a particular criminal case, non-disclosure of the Rickshaw driver's identity, failure to furnish the particulars of other passengers travelling in the Rickshaw from the District Court premises at Gul Kada to the place of occurrence, and omission to identify the persons who transported the deceased to the hospital for postmortem examination. However, the aforesaid objections, when examined in the backdrop of the entire prosecution evidence, predominantly pertain to collateral particulars rather than the essential Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din features of the occurrence. It is pertinent to observe that the witnesses entered the witness-box after a considerable interval of more than nine months from the occurrence, extending beyond a year in certain respects. In such circumstances, human memory cannot reasonably be expected to preserve and reproduce every incidental detail with mathematical precision. The lapse of time may naturally occasion discrepancies in recollection concerning peripheral matters, which do not necessarily impair the intrinsic worth of testimony otherwise found reliable. The touchstone for evaluating such discrepancies is whether they undermine the substratum of the prosecution case or materially dent the credibility of the witnesses regarding the identity of the assailant and his specific role in the commission of the offence. In the present case, unless the alleged omissions and inconsistencies are shown to affect these material aspects, they cannot, in isolation, furnish a legitimate ground for discarding the otherwise confidence-inspiring ocular account, more particularly that of natural narration of the occurrence furnished by none other than the minor Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din son of the deceased. Reference can be made to the case of “Khadim Hussain v/s State”, wherein the aforesaid rational of law has explicitly been explained qua creeping of minor contradiction with passage of time [ ]. Reliance can also be placed on the case of “Muhammad Ilyas v/s State” whereby it was held by apex Court that “contradictions which are not grave in nature can be ignored safely as minor contradictions creep in with passage of time” [ ]. Further reliance in this respect may also be placed on judgment of Hon’ble apex Court rendered in case titled “Zulfiqar Ahmad v/s State” reported as 2011 SCMR 492.

9. Learned counsel for the appellant also sought to impeach the veracity of the ocular account on the ground that both the prosecution eyewitnesses were closely related to the deceased, the complainant being her real brother and the minor witness her son. Although their consanguineous relationship with the deceased is an admitted feature of the case, such relationship, simpliciter, does not furnish a sound basis for discarding their testimony in toto. In the case of “Abdur Rauf v/s State”, it was expounded “Khadim Hussain v/s State” reported as PLD 2010 Supreme Court 669. “Muhammad Ilyas v/s State” reported as 2011 SCMR 460. Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din by Hon’ble apex Court that it is an intrinsic value of a statement of a prosecution witness which is to be taken into account and not his/her relationship. It is not a rule of thumb that an interested or related witness will always tell lie and independent witness truth rather testimony of a witness in each case is required to be adjudged in light of its own facts and circumstances. If it is established on record that a witness had a motive to implicate an accused person falsely in a case, then in such situation, independent corroboration may be sought from other evidence [ ].

Likewise, in the case of “Amal Sherin & another v/s State”, Hon’ble apex Court reiterated and followed the same rational of law to the effect that mere relationship of witnesses with the deceased would not detract from their veracity, who had absolutely no motive of their own to involve the accused [ ]. Same rational was also reiterated by apex Court in the case of “Khalid v/s State” by observing that in absence of any ulterior motive/animus for false implication of an accused, the confidence inspiring testimony of an eye-witness, whose presence with the deceased at the “Abdur Rauf v/s State & another” reported as 2003 SCMR 522. “Amal Sherin & another v/s State” reported as PLD 2004 Supreme Court 371. Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din time and place of occurrence is established, cannot be discarded merely due to his relationship with the deceased [ ]. Further reliance, in this regard, may be placed on the dicta expounded by apex Court in case titled “Zakir Khan and others Vs. The State” reported as 1995 SCMR 1793, in case titled “Salahud-Din & another v/s The State” reported as 2018 P Cr. LJ 1297 and case titled “Muhammad Umar v/s The State” reported as 2022 P Cr. LJ 695.

10. The medical evidence adduced by the prosecution lends substantial assurance to the ocular account regarding the situs, nature and character of the injury sustained by the deceased, Mst. Bakhti. Dr. Safia Shah, who stepped into the witness-box as PW-2, conducted the post-mortem examination and testified to the presence of a solitary firearm injury on the skull of the deceased, a vital and vulnerable part of the human anatomy. The medical findings, therefore, remain in accord with the prosecution's version that the deceased sustained a firearm injury to the head, which proved fatal. The medical evidence, thus, furnishes corroborative support to the “Khalid v/s State” reported as 2024 SCMR 1474. Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din ocular testimony of PW-3, Muhammad Khitab, the complainant, and PW-4, Hubaib, the minor eyewitness, insofar as the nature and location of the injury are concerned. The medical account is not at variance with the ocular version; rather, both strands of evidence are mutually consonant on this material aspect of the occurrence.

11. The ocular account finds further corroboration from the circumstantial evidence comprising the recovery of blood-stained earth and a crime empty of .30-bore from the place of occurrence, together with the blood-stained garments of the deceased. These recoveries lend additional corroborative force to the prosecution case. Of further significance is the recovery of the alleged weapon of offence, i.e., a .30-bore pistol, at the instance of the appellant. The forensic report, Ex.PW-11/29, furnishes a connecting link between the recovered crime empty and the weapon in question, as it records the opinion that the crime empty, marked as “C”, was of .30-bore and had been fired from .30-bore pistol No. A1326. The forensic findings, therefore, provide material corroboration to the prosecution version regarding the use of the Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din recovered weapon in the occurrence. Considered cumulatively with the ocular account and the other evidence on record, these circumstances lend further support to the prosecution case. The learned trial Court, therefore, rightly took these incriminating circumstances into consideration while assessing the appellant’s culpability.

12. Having sifted the prosecution evidence in its entirety and weighed its cumulative probative value, this Court finds that the charge against the appellant stands proved beyond reasonable doubt and that the finding of guilt recorded by the learned trial Court is not open to exception. The question of sentence, however, falls for distinct consideration. The evidence on record discloses that the appellant inflicted a single firearm injury upon the deceased and did not repeat the shot. Furthermore, the genesis of the occurrence was traceable to the deceased’s former matrimonial association with the appellant’s father and co-accused, Momin Khan, whereas no independent or compelling motive directly attributable to the appellant has been brought home through the evidence. It is also discernible from the prosecution version that, immediately after the occurrence, the injured deceased Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din was transported to the hospital by her brother, the complainant, where she later succumbed to her injury. In the ordinary course of such events, the possibility of the complainant’s garments being stained with blood while shifting or attending to the injured deceased cannot be discounted. Yet, the prosecution record is conspicuously silent as to the seizure of any such blood-stained garments by the Investigating Officer or their production before the trial Court. This omission does not, in isolation, demolish the prosecution case or impair the evidentiary worth of the otherwise reliable ocular account; nevertheless, it remains a circumstance relevant to the overall appraisal of the evidence. Taking into account the aforesaid features of the case, and keeping in view the settled distinction between the determination of culpability and the calibration of punishment, this Court is persuaded to commute the capital sentence awarded by the learned trial Court to a lesser sentence.

13. Thus, the minor discrepancies and lacunae in the prosecution evidence, as discussed hereinabove, do not suffice to warrant the outright acquittal of the appellant. However, these aspects may be taken into consideration while determining Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din the appropriate sentence, as observed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Mst. Bevi v. Ghulam Shabbir and another (1980 SCMR 859), wherein it was held as follows:- “It has been held in some cases that the principle underlying the concept of benefit of doubt can in addition to the consideration of question of guilt or otherwise, be pressed also in matter of sentence. As a definite motive was asserted against the respondent and the same has failed, keeping in view all the circumstances of this case, it would not be necessary to impose the capita' punishment. Therefore, while finding him guilty; under section 302, P. P. C. he is sentenced to transportation for life should be awarded as compensation.”

A similar principle was enunciated by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Mir Muhammad alias Miro v. State (2009 SCMR 1188). Reliance may also be placed on Muhammad Ayaz Khan v. Murtaza and others (2008 SCMR 984) and Kamran Ullah v. State and another (2020 SCMR 1214), wherein the Hon’ble apex Court further elucidated the relevant principles governing the appreciation of evidentiary deficiencies and their bearing on the question of sentence.

14. In view of the above discussion and exposition of law, the instant criminal appeal is partially allowed. The impugned judgment dated Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din 22.7.2025, passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge-VI/Judge, M.C.T.C./ I.Z.Q., Swat, in case FIR No.305 dated 21.03.2022, registered U/Ss 302 and 34, PPC, R/W section 19-AA, at Police Station Mingora, District Swat, is modified to the extent that the sentence of death awarded to the appellant/ convict, namely Iqbal son of Momin Khan, U/S 302(b), PPC, is converted into imprisonment for life, with the benefit of section 382-B, Cr.P.C. The remaining part of the impugned judgment dated 22.07.2025, particularly to the extent of imposition of compensation and conviction U/S 19-AA, shall remain intact. Murder Reference No.02-M of 2025 is answered in the negative.

15. So far as the connected Criminal Appeal No. 226-M of 2025, directed against the acquittal of accused/respondents No. 2 and 3, namely Israr and Momin Khan, is concerned, the record reveals that the allegations against them primarily pertain to their purported role in facilitating or abetting the commission of the offence, whereas no specific act of firing upon the Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din deceased has been ascribed to either of them. In the absence of any cogent and convincing evidence sufficient to dislodge the presumption of innocence fortified by their acquittal, no legal justification is made out for interference with the impugned judgment to their detriment. Accordingly, the acquittal recorded by the learned trial Court in favour of accused/respondents No. 2 and 3 is maintained, and the connected Criminal Appeal No. 226-M of 2025 is dismissed.
16. These are reasons of our short order of even date.
